rule.title: Firewall Rule Modified In The Windows Firewall Exception List
rule.author: frack113

es.summary: Se modificó una regla existente en la lista de excepciones de Windows Defender Firewall (Event ID 2005 en Windows 10, 2073 en Windows 11). Es una pista de hunting de severidad baja. Antes de cerrarla, confirme que el cambio era esperado.
es.what_it_detects: Eventos 2005/2073 de Firewall With Advanced Security, que registran el cambio de una regla de firewall existente. Se excluyen por ApplicationPath los cambios de Teams, Keybase, Messenger, Opera y Brave instalados por usuario.
es.why_it_matters: Un atacante que modifica una regla puede cambiar un bloqueo por un permiso, ampliar los puertos o las direcciones remotas, o hacer que una regla de confianza apunte a su propio binario. Así abre acceso entrante o tráfico de C2 sin crear reglas nuevas (debilitamiento de defensas, T1686.003).
triage_steps: Revise RuleName, RuleId, Direction, Action, LocalPorts, RemoteAddresses, Profiles y ApplicationPath. Anote si hay una regla que permite tráfico entrante, que abarca todos los puertos o que acepta cualquier dirección remota.
Identifique ModifyingUser y ModifyingApplication. Verifique si el cambio lo hizo netsh.exe, powershell.exe, mmc.exe, svchost (GPO/MDM) o un proceso inusual.
Busque los eventos 2004/2071 (alta) o 2005/2073 anteriores con el mismo RuleId y compare los valores anteriores con los nuevos.
Revise ApplicationPath: confirme si está firmado y si se ejecuta desde rutas con permiso de escritura para el usuario, como AppData, Temp o C:\Users\Public. Consulte su hash.
En el mismo host, en un rango de +/- 15 minutos, busque procesos con netsh advfirewall o Set-NetFirewallRule, servicios nuevos e inicios de sesión de ModifyingUser.
Busque conexiones entrantes nuevas o procesos en escucha en los puertos abiertos, y alertas previas del host o del usuario.
Compruebe si hay tickets de cambio, despliegues de GPO o Intune o actualizaciones de software que expliquen la modificación.
false_positives: Aplicaciones que actualizan sus propias reglas al instalarse o actualizarse, como navegadores, clientes de chat, juegos o agentes VPN.
Group Policy, Intune o SCCM aplicando cambios en la configuración del firewall.
Administradores que modifican reglas con wf.msc, netsh o PowerShell durante un mantenimiento aprobado.
Actualizaciones de Windows o de Defender que renuevan las reglas integradas.
response_steps: Confirme con el responsable o con el registro de cambios que el cambio estaba autorizado. Si lo estaba, cierre la alerta como benigna y ajuste la regla si el caso se repite.
Si el cambio no está autorizado, exporte la regla (Get-NetFirewallRule) como evidencia y luego reviértala o deshabilítela.
Aísle el host si la regla abre acceso entrante a un binario desconocido o si hay indicios de compromiso.
Investigue y elimine el binario de ApplicationPath y cualquier mecanismo de persistencia. Restablezca las credenciales de ModifyingUser si se usaron de forma indebida.
Restaure la línea base del firewall mediante GPO y vigile si el cambio vuelve a aparecer.
es.severity_rationale: La severidad baja es adecuada porque las reglas de firewall cambian a menudo por motivos legítimos y esta es una regla de hunting. Requiere contexto antes de escalar.

en.summary: An existing rule in the Windows Defender Firewall exception list was modified (Event ID 2005 on Windows 10, 2073 on Windows 11). This is a low-severity hunting lead. Confirm the change was expected before closing it.
en.what_it_detects: Firewall With Advanced Security events 2005/2073, which record a change to an existing firewall rule. Changes for Teams, Keybase, Messenger, Opera and Brave installed per user are excluded by ApplicationPath.
en.why_it_matters: Attackers who change a firewall rule can turn a block into an allow, widen ports or remote addresses, or point a trusted rule at their own binary. This lets them open inbound access or C2 traffic without adding a new rule (defense impairment, T1686.003).
triage_steps: Read RuleName, RuleId, Direction, Action, LocalPorts, RemoteAddresses, Profiles and ApplicationPath. Note any allow-inbound rule, rule covering all ports or rule open to any remote address.
Find ModifyingUser and ModifyingApplication. Check whether netsh.exe, powershell.exe, mmc.exe, svchost (GPO/MDM) or an unusual process made the change.
Look up the earlier 2004/2071 (added) or 2005/2073 events for the same RuleId and compare the old and new values.
Check ApplicationPath: is it signed, and does it run from a user-writable folder such as AppData, Temp or C:\Users\Public? Look up its hash.
On the same host within +/- 15 minutes, look for process creation with netsh advfirewall or Set-NetFirewallRule, new services, and logons by ModifyingUser.
Look for new inbound connections or listeners on the opened ports, and for earlier alerts on this host or user.
Check change tickets, GPO/Intune deployments and software updates that could explain the change.
false_positives: Applications that update their own firewall rules during installs or updates, such as browsers, chat clients, games or VPN agents.
Group Policy, Intune or SCCM pushing firewall configuration changes.
Administrators changing rules through wf.msc, netsh or PowerShell during approved maintenance.
Windows feature or Defender updates that refresh built-in rules.
response_steps: Confirm with the owner or change record that the change was authorized. Close the alert as benign and tune it if it recurs.
If the change is unauthorized, export the rule (Get-NetFirewallRule) as evidence. Then revert it or disable it.
Isolate the host if the rule opens inbound access to an unknown binary or there are signs of compromise.
Investigate and remove the binary in ApplicationPath and any persistence. Reset credentials for ModifyingUser if it was misused.
Restore the firewall baseline through GPO and watch for the change coming back.
en.severity_rationale: Low fits because firewall rules change often for legitimate reasons and this is a hunting rule. It needs context before anyone escalates.

positive.description: Windows 10 event 2005: an inbound rule was modified to allow a binary in C:\Users\Public on any port, changed by netsh.
Windows 11 event 2073: an RDP-related rule was widened to any remote address, changed through PowerShell.

negative.description: Event 2005 for the per-user Microsoft Teams install. ApplicationPath ends with the Teams path, so the optional filter excludes it (case-insensitive).
Event 2073 for the per-user Opera browser. ApplicationPath contains all three Opera filter strings, so the event is excluded.
